blocks.text: The same view was also favoured by Vossius, book 2, de Idololatria, ch. 4, and by Grotius on Matth. X, 25.; against them, however, several objections were raised by Selden, de Diis Syris, Syntagma 2, ch. 6, by Clericus in his Commentar. ad 2 Reg. I, 2., and by Jurieu in his Histor. Dogmatum et Cultuum vol. 4, tract. 4, ch. 3, p. 628 ff. — Drusius, in Matth. XII, 24., thinks that בעל זבוב, the god of flies, was so called from a resemblance he bore to a fly: For among the ancients, he adds, it was the custom to carve the statues of the gods in a form that represented a man in the body, but some animal in the head and face, say a bird, or a lion, or a fly; or conversely, it had a human face and represented some animal in the rest of the body; and he confirms this by the testimony of Porphyry from the book περι των ἐμψυχων ἀποχης [peri tōn empsychōn apochēs]. But this rests on mere conjecture, and a very uncertain one. — Simonis, in his Onomasticon Vet. Testam. p. 46, interprets זבוב as wandering, i.e. a crowd of men wandering hither and thither (compare Arabic ذبّ [dhabba], he wandered about without fixed abode), so that בעל זבוב would be the lord of wandering, i.e. the god of the Philistines as exiles, since they named almost all their things from exile and wandering, such as גרר, פלשת, אשדוד, עקרון etc. Nor is this interpretation of the word בעל זבוב wholly displeasing to J. D. Michaelis in the Supplemm. ad Lexx. Hebrr. vol. 1, p. 203, yet in such a way that he thinks בעל זבוב was a surname of Hercules, a deity of the Phoenicians, the same as Horace's wandering Hercules, because he had travelled through the whole world. — Joh. Alberti, in his Glossae N. T. p. 30, holds that בעל זבוב denotes καταπινοντα μυιας [katapinonta myias], swallowing flies, and that זבוב and בעל, which the Alexandrians rendered καταπινειν [katapinein] at Iesaj. XVI, 8., stands by metathesis of letters for בלע, he swallowed. Jac. Basnage, in his Antiqq. Iudaicc. vol. 1, believed that the God of hosts and of arms is designated by this name, because the Phoenicians could easily have turned the Hebrew צבאת into זבוב. — A new view was proposed by D. Mill in the dissertation de Beelzebub et Miphlezet, which is the sixth of his Dissertationes selectae, Utrecht 1724. He thinks the Phoenician בעל זבוב is the same as the Pluto of the Greeks, moved chiefly by this reason: that at Matth. XII, 24. and Luc. XI, 15. Βεελζεβουλ [Beelzeboul] or Βεελζεβουβ [Beelzeboub] is called ἀρχων δαιμονιων [archōn daimoniōn], prince of demons, and that such was Pluto, since he is called ἀρχων δαιμονων [archōn daimonōn] by Porphyry in Eusebius, Praeparat. Evangel. book 4, ch. 23, μεγαλοδαιμων [megalodaimōn] by Clement of Alexandria in the Protrept. ad Gentes p. 31, and βασιλευς ἐνερων [basileus enerōn], king of the underworld, by the Greek and Roman poets. Next, that to Beelzebub, as prince of demons, an immense power over demons is ascribed in the Gospels, and the same power is ascribed by the gentiles to Pluto, the ruler of demons. And just as people were wont to commend their welfare to Pluto, as lord of death, under whose rule were the Parcae, to whose decision the span of mortals' life was entrusted, and to vow victims to him, so Ahaziah, 2 Reg. I, 2., sent to inquire of Beelzebub about his health and life. Finally, that the meaning of the Hebrew or Phoenician name בעל זבוב also fits: for זבוב, which properly denotes any harmful insects, is often used by the Talmudic writers for demons; for instance in מדרש ילקוט שמעני, Midrasch Ialkut Simeoni section 2, fol. 14, col. 1, and section 3, fol. 111, col. 3, זבובין are evil demons; hence בעל זבוב is rightly explained in the Gospels as ἀρχων δαιμονιων [archōn daimoniōn]. But this whole view of Mill [III, 351] seems more ingenious and contrived than true. — For Noldius, in the Notes and Vindicc. ad Concordantt. Particularr. note 636, p. 802, Tympe's edition, Βεελζεβουβ [Beelzeboub] in the N. T. is not the same as בעל זבוב, the god of the Ekronites, but the Syriac ܒܥܠܕܒܒܐ ܒܥܠ ܕܒܒܐ, adversary, enemy, or διαβολος [diabolos], Σατανᾶς [Satanas]; this view also pleased Storr, who in his Dissertat. de sensu historico p. 38 holds that Jesus was called by this name by the Jews because they considered him an enemy of the ancestral religion, compare Ioh. VII, 12. 47. VIII, 48. IX, 28. The chief obstacle to this view is that the genuine reading in the N. T. is not Βεελζεβουβ [Beelzeboub], as the Vulgate, altered by Jerome, has together with the Old Syriac, but Βεελζεβουλ [Beelzeboul]; this reading is constant in all the Greek codices consulted so far, and is also rendered by the Greek fathers, e.g. Theophylact, and by the versions: the Old Latin before Jerome, the Saxon, Gothic, Coptic, the later Syriac, the Russian, and both Arabic ones, that in the Polyglots and that edited by Erpenius.
